title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the weight of a punishment, the tense of a report

questions.prompt: A mother writes to the education office about her son: "He cannot follow what the class says, the other children have grown impatient with him, and he no longer believes he is able to do anything at all." Which word of the module names what the boy has lost?

options.text: his impairment
his plight
his qualifications
his self-esteem

questions.explanation: Self-esteem is the value a person puts on himself, and the last clause of the letter describes exactly its collapse. An impairment is the difficulty he lives with, so it is the cause of the trouble and not something he has lost. A plight is the serious and difficult situation he is now in — that is something he has acquired, not something taken from him. And nothing in the letter concerns certificates, which is what qualifications would name.

questions.prompt: The newspaper article of the module ends by saying that where there was more praise, fewer children were mucking around. What were those children doing?

options.text: asking the teacher too many questions
copying the work of the pupil beside them
leaving the room without permission
wasting time instead of working

questions.explanation: To muck around is to waste time instead of getting on with the work, and it is the informal expression the article uses for the ordinary low-level disruption of a class. It does not mean cheating, which is what copying a neighbour would be, nor walking out, which is a far heavier matter than the article is discussing. Asking questions, however many, is not disruption at all — it is the behaviour the researchers say a teacher should be looking for.

questions.prompt: A school lists its four punishments in its rules. Arrange them from the lightest to the heaviest.

options.text: lines — the pupil copies out the same sentence a hundred times on a sheet of paper
detention — the pupil is kept back at the end of the day, or called in on Sunday to work
suspension — the pupil attends no lesson until the school has met about his case
exclusion — the pupil does not come back, and another school or another way of studying has to be found

questions.explanation: The four rise by what each one takes away. Lines take only a sheet of paper and an hour at home, and the pupil misses nothing at school, so they come first. Detention takes his own time instead — the end of the day, or a Sunday — but he is still in his lessons, so it stands above lines and below everything that touches the lessons themselves. Suspension takes the lessons away, and it does so for a limited period, until the school has met about the case, so it comes above detention. Exclusion takes the school away for good and forces the family to find another one, which is why nothing can stand above it.

questions.prompt: Four words of this module: education, detention, suspension, destination. Which syllable carries the main stress in all four of them?

options.text: the first syllable of the word, whichever word it is
the syllable just in front of the ending
the last syllable, the ending itself
a different syllable in each of the four words

questions.explanation: Say them aloud and the same beat lands each time: edu-CA-tion, de-TEN-tion, sus-PEN-sion, desti-NA-tion. In almost every word ending in -tion or -sion the main stress falls on the syllable immediately in front of that ending. The ending itself is never stressed, and the first syllable carries the stress only in an exception such as TELevision. The answer that gives each word its own pattern is the belief the exercise exists to correct: this is one of the few places in English where a written ending predicts the beat reliably.

questions.prompt: A pupil's report on a book has already given the type of book, where the story is set, who the main characters are, and the whole of the plot in order. According to the plan of the module, what is still missing?

options.text: the type of book, the setting and the main characters
the events of the story, in the order in which they happen
what she thought of it, and whether she would recommend it
the name of the author and the number of pages in her edition

questions.explanation: The plan has three parts: an introduction that names the type of book, the setting and the characters, a body that tells the plot in order, and a conclusion that gives the writer's own judgement and her recommendation. The first two have been written, so the conclusion is what is left — and it is the part the task depends on, since the report is meant to make other pupils want to read the book. The introduction and the body are exactly what she has already written, so neither of them can be what is missing. The author and the number of pages appear nowhere in the plan; they belong to a bibliography, not to a report.

questions.prompt: Four sentences taken from one report on a book. One of them is in the wrong tense for the part of the report it belongs to. Which one?

options.text: The story is set in a mining village in the north of England.
The main character was a young teacher who arrives in the village in September.
I read it in three evenings and I found the ending a little predictable.
I recommend it to anybody who has ever had to change school in the middle of a year.

questions.explanation: The plot and everything the book contains are reported in the simple present, and the fault is visible inside the sentence itself: was and arrives describe the same person in the same breath, one in the past and one in the present. Written correctly it reads: the main character is a young teacher who arrives in the village in September. The setting takes the same present, so the sentence about the mining village is right. The sentence about the three evenings is right too, but for the opposite reason: it reports what the reader did, and the reading really is over. And the recommendation is made now, so it stays in the present.
